document_title: Statement by Prime Minister Tomiichi Murayama "On the occasion of the 50th anniversary of the war's end" (15 August 1995)
response_text:
Statement by Prime Minister Tomiichi Murayama
"On the occasion of the 50th anniversary of the war's end"
(15 August 1995)
(Translation)

The world has seen fifty years elapse since the war came to an end. Now, when I remember the many people both at home and abroad who fell victim to war, my heart is overwhelmed by a flood of emotions.

The peace and prosperity of today were built as Japan overcame great difficulty to arise from a devastated land after defeat in the war. That achievement is something of which we are proud, and let me herein express my heartfelt admiration for the wisdom and untiring effort of each and every one of our citizens. Let me also express once again my profound gratitude for the indispensable support and assistance extended to Japan by the countries of the world, beginning with the United States of America. I am also delighted that we have been able to build the friendly relations which we enjoy today with the neighboring countries of the Asia-Pacific region, the United States and the countries of Europe.

Now that Japan has come to enjoy peace and abundance, we tend to overlook the pricelessness and blessings of peace. Our task is to convey to younger generations the horrors of war, so that we never repeat the errors in our history. I believe that, as we join hands, especially with the peoples of neighboring countries, to ensure true peace in the Asia-Pacific region -indeed, in the entire world- it is necessary, more than anything else, that we foster relations with all countries based on deep understanding and trust. Guided by this conviction, the Government has launched the Peace, Friendship and Exchange Initiative, which consists of two parts promoting: support for historical research into relations in the modern era between Japan and the neighboring countries of Asia and elsewhere; and rapid expansion of exchanges with those countries. Furthermore, I will continue in all sincerity to do my utmost in efforts being made on the issues arisen from the war, in order to further strengthen the relations of trust between Japan and those countries.

Now, upon this historic occasion of the 50th anniversary of the war's end, we should bear in mind that we must look into the past to learn from the lessons of history, and ensure that we do not stray from the path to the peace and prosperity of human society in the future.

During a certain period in the not too distant past, Japan, following a mistaken national policy, advanced along the road to war, only to ensnare the Japanese people in a fateful crisis, and, through its colonial rule and aggression, caused tremendous damage and suffering to the people of many countries, particularly to those of Asian nations. In the hope that no such mistake be made in the future, I regard, in a spirit of humility, these irrefutable facts of history, and express here once again my feelings of deep remorse and state my heartfelt apology. Allow me also to express my feelings of profound mourning for all victims, both at home and abroad, of that history.

Building from our deep remorse on this occasion of the 50th anniversary of the end of the war, Japan must eliminate self-righteous nationalism, promote international coordination as a responsible member of the international community and, thereby, advance the principles of peace and democracy. At the same time, as the only country to have experienced the devastation of atomic bombing, Japan, with a view to the ultimate elimination of nuclear weapons, must actively strive to further global disarmament in areas such as the strengthening of the nuclear non-proliferation regime. It is my conviction that in this way alone can Japan atone for its past and lay to rest the spirits of those who perished.

It is said that one can rely on good faith. And so, at this time of remembrance, I declare to the people of Japan and abroad my intention to make good faith the foundation of our Government policy, and this is my vow.

document_title: Policy Speech by Prime Minister Morihiro Hosokawa to the 127th Session of the National Diet
response_text:
Policy Speech by Prime Minister Morihiro Hosokawa to the 127th Session of the National Diet
(23 August 1993)

[...]

Forty-eight years later, Japan has now become one of the prime beneficiaries of world prosperity and peace. Yet we should never forget that this achievement rests upon the supreme sacrifices made during the war and is the result of the great efforts made by previous generations. I believe it is important at this juncture that we state clearly before all the world our remorse at our past history and our renewed determination to do better. I would thus like to take this opportunity to express anew our profound remorse and apologies for the fact that past Japanese actions, including aggression and colonial rule, caused unbearable suffering and sorrow for so many people and to state that we will demonstrate our new determination by contributing more than ever before to world peace.

[The speech otherwise addresses disaster relief, political reform, the economy, and foreign policy generally; only this passage concerns historical recognition. Full text retrieved and reviewed in both English and the Japanese original.]
relevant_excerpt: I would thus like to take this opportunity to express anew our profound remorse and apologies for the fact that past Japanese actions, including aggression and colonial rule, caused unbearable suffering and sorrow for so many people and to state that we will demonstrate our new determination by contributing more than ever before to world peace.
coder_notes: First formal Japanese-government acknowledgment of the war as one of "aggression" (shinryaku), delivered as the historical-recognition passage within an otherwise general Diet policy speech by the first non-LDP postwar Prime Minister. Widely credited by historians as having opened the way for the 1995 Murayama Danwa. document_title: Statement of Prime Minister Junichiro Koizumi [on the Yasukuni Shrine visit]
response_text:
Statement of Prime Minister Junichiro Koizumi
(13 August 2001)

The day after tomorrow, August 15, is the fifty-sixth anniversary of the end of the war. Looking back to the last war at the very beginning of the twenty-first century, solemn feelings fill my heart. During the war, Japan caused tremendous sufferings to many people of the world including its own people. Following a mistaken national policy during a certain period in the past, Japan imposed, through its colonial rule and aggression, immeasurable ravages and suffering particularly to the people of the neighboring countries in Asia. This has left a still incurable scar to many people in the region.

Sincerely facing these deeply regrettable historical facts as they are, here I offer my feelings of profound remorse and sincere mourning to all the victims of the war.

I believe that Japan must never again proceed a path to war. [...] I had thought that people of Japan and those of the neighboring countries would understand my belief if it was fully explained, and thus, after my assumption of office as Prime Minister, I expressed my wish to visit Yasukuni Shrine on August 15.

However, as the anniversary of the end of the war came closer, vocal debates have started at home and abroad as to whether I should visit Yasukuni Shrine. [...] I have made my own decision not to visit Yasukuni Shrine on that day, and I would like to choose another day for a visit.

[Remainder of statement discusses the political controversy over the deferred visit and the Prime Minister's intention to discuss the matter with Chinese and Korean leaders.]
relevant_excerpt: Following a mistaken national policy during a certain period in the past, Japan imposed, through its colonial rule and aggression, immeasurable ravages and suffering particularly to the people of the neighboring countries in Asia. This has left a still incurable scar to many people in the region. Sincerely facing these deeply regrettable historical facts as they are, here I offer my feelings of profound remorse and sincere mourning to all the victims of the war.
coder_notes: Issued the day Koizumi announced he would defer his planned August 15 Yasukuni Shrine visit amid domestic/international controversy (he visited instead on August 13). Notable for using the standard "remorse" formula (shinryaku/colonial-rule acknowledgment) without the word "apology" appearing anywhere in the text -- coded apology=0 on that basis, unlike Murayama/Hosokawa/Obuchi which explicitly use "apology"/"apologize". Selected as a landmark anchor for the Yasukuni dimension of the reviewer-requested timeline, and because the Yasukuni-visit political dynamic (domestic conservative base vs. diplomatic cost with China/Korea) is a clear kingdon_politics=1 case. Page itself cites "[Source] Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Japan". [...]

Prime Minister Obuchi, looking back on the relations between Japan and the Republic of Korea during this century, regarded in a spirit of humility the fact of history that Japan caused, during a certain period in the past, tremendous damage and suffering to the people of the Republic of Korea through its colonial rule, and expressed his deep remorse and heartfelt apology for this fact.

document_title: Statement by Prime Minister Shinzo Abe [on the 70th anniversary of the end of World War II]
response_text:
Statement by Prime Minister Shinzo Abe (14 August 2015)

[...]

Incident, aggression, war -- we shall never again resort to any form of the threat or use of force as a means of settling international disputes. We shall abandon colonial rule forever and respect the right of self-determination of all peoples throughout the world.

With deep repentance for the war, Japan made that pledge. [...]

Japan has repeatedly expressed the feelings of deep remorse and heartfelt apology for its actions during the war. In order to manifest such feelings through concrete actions, we have engraved in our hearts the histories of suffering of the people in Asia as our neighbours: those in Southeast Asian countries such as Indonesia and the Philippines, and Taiwan, the Republic of Korea and China, among others; and we have consistently devoted ourselves to the peace and prosperity of the region since the end of the war.

Such position articulated by the previous cabinets will remain unshakable into the future.

[...]

In Japan, the postwar generations now exceed eighty per cent of its population. We must not let our children, grandchildren, and even further generations to come, who have nothing to do with that war, be predestined to apologize. Still, even so, we Japanese, across generations, must squarely face the history of the past. We have the responsibility to inherit the past, in all humbleness, and pass it on to the future.

[...] We shall never forget that there were women behind the battlefields whose honour and dignity were severely injured.
relevant_excerpt: Japan has repeatedly expressed the feelings of deep remorse and heartfelt apology for its actions during the war. [...] Such position articulated by the previous cabinets will remain unshakable into the future. [...] We must not let our children, grandchildren, and even further generations to come, who have nothing to do with that war, be predestined to apologize.
coder_notes: The last cabinet-decided decennial Danwa to date (see the companion 2025 Ishiba record, which was explicitly NOT issued as a cabinet-decided Danwa). apology=0 and remorse=0 are deliberate, NOT an oversight: this statement does not itself offer a fresh first-person apology or remorse -- it REAFFIRMS that "Japan has repeatedly expressed" these feelings in the past and declares that position "unshakable," then pivots to argue that future generations "must not...be predestined to apologize." This is the well-documented "Did Abe apologize?" ambiguity (see e.g. The Diplomat, 2015-08-14, title of that name) and is coded here the same way this corpus codes every other reaffirmation-only statement (e.g. all 2020-2025 Japan main-axis records, which show the identical reaffirm-but-do-not-restate pattern and are likewise coded apology=0/remorse=0): a reference to a past apology is not itself a new apology. Coded explicitly this way for direct comparability with the main-axis coding convention; see pilot_coverage_report.md's Aug 15 timeline section for the full argument that 2015 is the pivot point after which Japan's official repertoire shifts from (occasionally) offering apology/remorse to only ever reaffirming it. institution: Prime Minister of Japan (personal reflection, NOT a Cabinet decision)
document_title: Reflection by Prime Minister: On the 80th anniversary of the end of the war
response_text:
Reflection by Prime Minister: On the 80th anniversary of the end of the war (10 October 2025)

(This provisional translation is subject to further edits.)

80 years have passed since the end of the war. [...]

To date, Statements by the Prime Minister have been issued on the 50th, 60th and 70th anniversary of the end of the war, and I uphold the positions articulated by the previous cabinets on history. The past three Statements do not specifically address in depth why we could not have avoided the war. [...] The unanswered question is: why our domestic political system could not serve as a brake to stop such attempts.

[The remainder of the document -- the great majority of its length -- is a detailed historical analysis of Imperial Japan's own constitutional, governmental, parliamentary, and media failures to maintain civilian control over the military in the 1920s-1940s (the Meiji Constitution's divided command authority, the 1940 expulsion of Diet member Saito Takao for an anti-war speech, wartime press self-censorship, etc.), concluding with lessons for present-day civilian control of Japan's Self-Defense Forces. It does not at any point mention Korea, China, colonial rule, comfort women, forced labor, or any historical wrong committed against another country's people -- its sole reference to the wider region is a passing mention of a memorial visit to a Japanese war-dead cemetery in the Philippines.]

I believe that the foundation of our nation as a peace-loving nation will be further strengthened by having every citizen, including the younger generation, proactively reflect on the previous war and the nature of peace, and apply these lessons to the future.

October 10, 2025
Prime Minister
ISHIBA Shigeru
relevant_excerpt: To date, Statements by the Prime Minister have been issued on the 50th, 60th and 70th anniversary of the end of the war, and I uphold the positions articulated by the previous cabinets on history. The past three Statements do not specifically address in depth why we could not have avoided the war. [...] The unanswered question is: why our domestic political system could not serve as a brake to stop such attempts.
coder_notes: This is the 80th-anniversary document in the 50/60/70-year Danwa sequence (Murayama 1995, Koizumi 2005 [not yet collected], Abe 2015), but it was explicitly NOT issued as a cabinet-decided Danwa: contemporary Japanese reporting (e.g. Tokyo Shimbun, 2025-10-11; Nikkei, 2025-09-24; JCP/Akahata, 2025-10-11) confirms Ishiba originally intended a cabinet-decided statement but abandoned that plan after opposition from within the LDP, releasing this lesser "naikaku soridaijin shokan" (Reflection by the Prime Minister) instead -- a personal document with no cabinet endorsement. agency_explicit/attribution_direction/responsibility_actor are coded NA, not 0, because the document does not engage the Japan-vs-Asia-neighbors historical-wrong question AT ALL (contrast Abe 2015, which engages it but only reaffirms a past apology): this document reframes "historical recognition" entirely as a question of Imperial Japan's own domestic constitutional/ civilian-control failure, with zero mention of Korea, China, colonial rule, or any other-directed wrongdoing -- a genre AND framing shift beyond even the attenuation seen in Abe 2015.
